automountServiceAccountToken.description:
Mount the ServiceAccount API token into the pod. Set on the pod itself, which is what
actually keeps the token out of the container: the ServiceAccount-level setting is ignored as
soon as a pod names a different account.
automountServiceAccountToken.title: automountServiceAccountToken

backup.description:
Scheduled logical backups, taken with the `document_exporter` management command. This is a
different kind of backup from a volume snapshot and neither replaces the other: a snapshot is a
crash-consistent copy of bytes that restores onto the same engine at a compatible version, while
an export is documents plus a `manifest.json` that can be imported into a *fresh* instance — the
only form that survives a move to another cluster or the SQLite to PostgreSQL switch.

The exporter takes the application's own media lock while it runs, so it does not race the
consumer for files. It is not a transactional snapshot of the database, though, so schedule it
for a quiet hour.

activeDeadlineSeconds.description:
Seconds a run may take before it is killed. Six hours covers a first full export of a large
archive over slow storage; without it a wedged export blocks every later run under
`concurrencyPolicy: Forbid`.
activeDeadlineSeconds.title: activeDeadlineSeconds

backoffLimit.description:
Retries before a run is given up on. Low on purpose: an export that failed on a full volume
or an unreachable database fails the same way three seconds later, and the next scheduled run
is the real retry.
backoffLimit.title: backoffLimit

coScheduleWithApp.description:
Schedule the backup pod onto the node the application pod is running on, with a required
`podAffinity`.

This is what makes the default `ReadWriteOnce` claims work: an RWO volume can be mounted by
several pods at once as long as they share a node, and cannot be attached to two nodes at all.
With this off and RWO storage, the Job either happens to land correctly or sits Pending until
its deadline — a backup that silently never runs.

The cost is that a backup cannot start while the application pod is down, which is the right
trade: it would have nothing consistent to read anyway. Turn it off for `ReadWriteMany`
storage, or when `backup.affinity` states the placement explicitly.
coScheduleWithApp.title: coScheduleWithApp

concurrencyPolicy.description:
What to do when a run is still going at the next scheduled time. `Forbid` is the only safe
answer here: two exporters writing one target directory interleave their output, and the
second one's `--delete` pass removes files the first has not written yet.
concurrencyPolicy.title: concurrencyPolicy

enabled.description:
Create the backup CronJob. Requires `persistence.export.enabled`, because the Job would
otherwise write the archive into its own `emptyDir` and delete it again on completion — a
backup that reports success nightly and restores nothing. The chart refuses to render rather
than producing that.
enabled.title: enabled

existingSecretKey.description: Key inside `existingSecret` that holds the export passphrase.
existingSecretKey.title: existingSecretKey

failedJobsHistoryLimit.description:
Failed Jobs retained in the CronJob's history. Keep at least a couple: the failed Job's pod
is the only place the reason is recorded.
failedJobsHistoryLimit.title: failedJobsHistoryLimit

mode.description:
What kind of export to take.

`incremental` keeps one continuously-updated export tree in the target directory, re-writing
only the documents that changed since the last run. Cheapest by far, and the right default —
but it is one snapshot, not a history, so a document deleted by mistake is gone from the
backup on the next run.

`zip` produces a dated archive per run and keeps `backup.zip.retentionCount` of them, which is
what gives you a history to roll back to. **It builds the whole export in the scratch
directory first**, so it needs as much free space there as the entire archive occupies; see
`backup.scratch`.

`dataOnly` exports the database contents and no files at all. Small and quick, and useful
alongside a volume snapshot that already covers the media — but on its own it restores an
instance that knows about every document and holds none of them.
mode.title: mode

nodeSelector.description: Node selector for the backup pod. Empty inherits the application's.
nodeSelector.title: nodeSelector

options.description:
The exporter's own flags. Every one of these is a documented `document_exporter` option;
the names here are the long forms.

batchSize.description:
`--batch-size`: database records serialised per batch. Lower it if the Job is killed for
exceeding its memory limit on a large archive.
batchSize.title: batchSize

compareChecksums.description:
`--compare-checksums`: decide what changed by hashing file contents rather than by
comparing size and modification time. Slower on every run, and the only setting that
notices a file corrupted in place.
compareChecksums.title: compareChecksums

compareJson.description:
`--compare-json`: leave the manifest and metadata JSON files alone when their contents
have not changed, which keeps an incremental export's modification times stable for a
file-level backup tool watching the directory.
compareJson.title: compareJson

delete.description:
`--delete`: remove exported files that are no longer in the dataset, so the target tracks
the archive rather than growing forever. Meaningless in `zip` mode, where the same flag
instead empties the target directory before the new archive is moved in — which would
destroy every retained archive, so the chart refuses to render that combination.
delete.title: delete

noArchive.description:
`--no-archive`: leave out the generated PDF/A files. They are reproducible from the
originals by re-running OCR, so this trades a much smaller backup for a long restore.
noArchive.title: noArchive

noThumbnail.description: `--no-thumbnail`: leave out thumbnails, which are regenerated on demand.
noThumbnail.title: noThumbnail

splitManifest.description:
`--split-manifest`: write one JSON file per document rather than a single `manifest.json`.
Worth setting for a large archive — a monolithic manifest is one enormous file that a
deduplicating backup tool has to re-transfer whenever any document changes.
splitManifest.title: splitManifest

useFilenameFormat.description:
`--use-filename-format`: name exported files with `paperless.filenameFormat` instead of
the exporter's own scheme. Makes the export browsable by a human; makes it less stable,
because renaming a correspondent renames files.
useFilenameFormat.title: useFilenameFormat

useFolderPrefix.description:
`--use-folder-prefix`: sort the export into `archive/`, `originals/`, `thumbnails/` and
`json/` subdirectories instead of interleaving them.
useFolderPrefix.title: useFolderPrefix

options.title: options

passphrase.description:
Passphrase encrypting the sensitive fields of the export. Ignored when `existingSecret` is
set. It reaches the exporter through an environment variable rather than on the command line,
so it does not appear in the pod spec or in `kubectl describe`.

**Store it somewhere other than the backup.** An encrypted export whose passphrase is lost is
not a backup, and the same passphrase has to be given to `restore` on the way back in.
passphrase.title: passphrase

podAnnotations.description: Additional annotations for the backup pod.
podAnnotations.title: podAnnotations

podLabels.description: Additional labels for the backup pod.
podLabels.title: podLabels

schedule.description: Cron schedule. The default is nightly at 03:00, which is the quiet hour this wants.
schedule.title: schedule

scratch.description:
Scratch space for the backup pod, mounted at `/tmp` as `PAPERLESS_SCRATCH_DIR`.

Separate from `persistence.scratchSizeLimit` because the requirement differs by orders of
magnitude. An incremental export streams straight into the target and needs almost none; a
`zip` export assembles the **entire** export tree here before compressing it, so it needs as
much free space as the whole archive occupies. An `emptyDir` is charged against the node's
ephemeral storage, and a pod that exceeds its limit is evicted mid-export.

existingClaim.description:
Use an existing PersistentVolumeClaim for the scratch directory instead of an `emptyDir`.
This is the answer for `zip` mode over an archive larger than the node's ephemeral storage.
existingClaim.title: existingClaim

sizeLimit.description:
Size limit of the `emptyDir`. Empty removes the limit, which is the default here because
a limit too small for the archive turns a backup into an eviction. Ignored when
`existingClaim` is set.
sizeLimit.title: sizeLimit

scratch.title: scratch

startingDeadlineSeconds.description:
Seconds a missed schedule may still be started within. Bounded rather than unlimited so a
controller outage does not fire every skipped run at once when it comes back.
startingDeadlineSeconds.title: startingDeadlineSeconds

successfulJobsHistoryLimit.description: Completed Jobs retained in the CronJob's history.
successfulJobsHistoryLimit.title: successfulJobsHistoryLimit

suspend.description: Suspend the schedule without deleting the CronJob, for a maintenance window.
suspend.title: suspend

target.description: Directory the export is written to, inside the export volume.
target.title: target

timeZone.description:
IANA time zone the schedule is interpreted in (`Europe/Berlin`). Empty uses the
kube-controller-manager's zone, which is UTC on most clusters. Requires Kubernetes 1.27+; on
older clusters the field is dropped rather than rejected.
timeZone.title: timeZone

tolerations.description: Tolerations for the backup pod. Empty inherits the application's.
tolerations.title: tolerations

ttlSecondsAfterFinished.description:
Seconds a finished Job is kept before the TTL controller removes it. A day, so the logs of
last night's backup are still there in the morning.
ttlSecondsAfterFinished.title: ttlSecondsAfterFinished

upload.description:
Ship the finished export off the cluster. An export sitting on a PersistentVolume in the
same cluster as the archive it backs up survives a mistake, but not the cluster.

The chart deliberately takes no dependency on any particular tool. When this is enabled the
exporter moves to an `initContainer` and the container below becomes the pod's main container
— so it runs only after the export has completed successfully, with the export volume mounted.
Any image that can copy a directory somewhere (rclone, restic, the AWS CLI, `mc`) works, with
its own credentials from its own Secret.

container.description:
The container itself, in the `corev1.Container` shape, verbatim apart from the export
volume mount the chart appends. `name` and `image` are required; everything else — `command`,
`env`, `envFrom`, `resources`, `securityContext` — is yours. Required when
`backup.upload.enabled` is set. Rendered through the template engine, so
`{{ .Release.Name }}` works.

Typed against the Kubernetes definition would be better, but a `$ref` to it makes the empty
default itself invalid — `name` is a required property — so the object is left open and
`validateValues` checks what actually matters instead.
container.title: container

enabled.description: Run the upload container after each successful export.
enabled.title: enabled

mountPath.description: Where the export volume is mounted in the upload container.
mountPath.title: mountPath

upload.title: upload

nameTemplate.description:
Base name of each archive, as a `strftime` format string; `.zip` is appended. Expanded by
`date` **inside the container at run time**, not by Helm — a name templated at render time
would be frozen at the moment of the last `helm upgrade`, and every run would overwrite the
same file.
nameTemplate.title: nameTemplate

retentionCount.description:
How many archives to keep. After a successful export the oldest are deleted until this
many remain, so the export volume has to hold this many copies of the archive.
retentionCount.title: retentionCount

gateway.description:
Gateway API configuration, consumed by `common.gateway.*`. The successor to `ingress`, and
an independent switch from it: a cluster migrating between an Ingress controller and a Gateway
implementation runs both for a while.

The division of labour is the API's, not this chart's. A `Gateway` — the listeners, the
address, the certificates — belongs to the cluster operator; an application owns only the
`HTTPRoute` that attaches to it. So the default here is route-only, and `create` is for
installs that have no cluster-wide Gateway to attach to.

addresses.description: Addresses requested for the created Gateway, e.g. a fixed `IPAddress`.
addresses.title: addresses

annotations.description: Annotations for the HTTPRoute and the created Gateway. Values may contain Go templates.
annotations.title: annotations

backendRefs.description:
Backends for rules that name none. Defaults to this chart's own Service. Weights are
honoured, so a traffic split needs no custom rule.
backendRefs.title: backendRefs

create.description:
Also create the Gateway itself. Leave off when the cluster already runs one — that is the
normal case, and one Gateway per application usually means one load balancer per
application. When on, a route that names no parent attaches to it automatically.
create.title: create

GatewayClass that programs the created Gateway, e.g. `cilium`, `istio`, `envoy-gateway`,
`nginx`. Required by `create`; a Gateway without one is never reconciled. Ignored otherwise.
gatewayClassName.title: gatewayClassName

hostnames.description:
Hostnames the route serves. Values may contain Go templates.

Required unless `create` is set. A route with no hostnames matches every name its listener
accepts: on a Gateway this chart owns that is harmless, and sometimes the point — an install
reached by address has no DNS name to state. On a shared Gateway it means taking over traffic
meant for other applications, so the render refuses it.
hostnames.title: hostnames

controller-specific annotation; Gateway API expresses it as a typed `RequestRedirect`

sectionName.description:
Listener to bind the redirect to. Must be the plaintext one: attached to every listener,
the redirect would also apply to the HTTPS listener and loop forever. Defaults to `http`,
the name of the listener `create` renders.
sectionName.title: sectionName

httpsRedirect.title: httpsRedirect

listeners.description:
Listeners for the created Gateway, replacing the derived ones entirely. Reach for this
when a listener needs its own hostname or certificate.

parentRefs.description:
Gateways the route attaches to. Each entry takes `name` and optionally `namespace`,
`sectionName` (a single listener), `port`, `group` and `kind`; the API's defaults are filled
in. Values may contain Go templates.

A route that names no parent is accepted by the API server and then does nothing — no
listener ever programs it — so this is required unless `create` is set.
Example:
```yaml
parentRefs:
  - name: shared-gateway
    namespace: gateway-system
    sectionName: https
```
parentRefs.title: parentRefs

path.title: path

rules.description:
Routing rules, in full `HTTPRouteRule` form (`matches`, `filters`, `backendRefs`,

only narrows the path does not have to restate where the traffic goes.

Left empty, the route gets one rule matching `path` as a prefix — the Gateway API equivalent
of a single-path Ingress, and a complete configuration together with `hostnames`.
rules.title: rules

TLS for the created Gateway's HTTPS listener. Ignored without `create`, and irrelevant
when attaching to somebody else's Gateway — the certificate is theirs.

networkPolicy.description:
Network policy configuration.

Every generated egress rule is scoped by a `to:` selector. An egress rule that lists only
ports is not a restriction — the NetworkPolicy API reads a missing `to` as "any
destination", so such a policy permits traffic to every in-cluster service and to the
cloud metadata endpoint.

cilium.description:
Cilium-only additions, used when `engine` is `cilium` or `both`. Everything above is
translated into the CiliumNetworkPolicy automatically; these are the rules the portable API
has no way to express.

`extraIngress`, `extraEgress` and the per-section `customRules` above are *not* carried over:
those are verbatim `networking.k8s.io/v1` rule objects and are not valid CNP. The fields
below are their counterparts.

description.description:
`spec.description`, which Cilium surfaces in `cilium policy get` and in Hubble flow
verdicts. The one place to record *why* a rule exists where an operator debugging a drop
will actually see it.
description.title: description

customRules.description: Additional egress rules in CiliumNetworkPolicy form, appended verbatim.
customRules.title: customRules

dnsMatchPatterns.description:
What the DNS proxy may resolve, e.g. `- matchPattern: "*.example.com"`. Defaults to
everything, which only permits the lookup — an answer is still only reachable if some
rule allows the address.
dnsMatchPatterns.title: dnsMatchPatterns

entityPorts.description: Restrict the `toEntities` rule to specific ports. Empty means all ports.
entityPorts.title: entityPorts

fqdnPorts.description: Ports the `toFQDNs` rule allows. Defaults to TCP/443.
fqdnPorts.title: fqdnPorts

httpRules.description:
L7 HTTP rules layered onto the `toFQDNs` rule, e.g.
`- method: GET` / `path: "/v1/.*"`. Turns "may reach this host" into "may make these
requests to this host". Costs a proxy hop per connection.
httpRules.title: httpRules

toEntities.description:
Named destination sets, e.g. `world` for everything outside the cluster, or
`kube-apiserver`. Not a synonym for the `egress.cidr`/`except` translation: `world` does
not carve out the cloud metadata endpoint the way those defaults do.
toEntities.title: toEntities

toFQDNs.description:
Destinations by name rather than by address, e.g. `- matchName: api.example.com` or
`- matchPattern: "*.example.com"`. This is the rule the CIDR-based `egress.https` was
always a poor approximation of: "may reach the internet on 443" permits every public host
that exists, where this permits the ones the application actually talks to.

Enforced against the addresses Cilium's DNS proxy saw returned for the name, so
`egress.dns.enabled` must stay on — the render fails if it is not.
toFQDNs.title: toFQDNs

restore.description:
Importing an export produced by `document_exporter`, whether from a backup of this instance or
from a different paperless-ngx altogether.

This is deliberately not a Job. `document_importer` needs the media and data directories to
itself and has to finish before anything else touches them, which no separately-scheduled pod can
promise — so the import runs as an `initContainer` on the application pod, ahead of the
webserver, the consumer and the scheduler. That gives it exclusive access without a second copy
of the volumes, works under `ReadWriteOnce`, and fails the pod rather than starting a
half-imported archive.

It runs once, guarded by a marker file on the data volume, and is a no-op on every start after
that — so these values can be left in place instead of being removed in a follow-up upgrade.

Importing a `.zip` export extracts it in full to the scratch directory first, so
`persistence.scratchSizeLimit` has to be at least the archive's uncompressed size or the pod is
evicted part-way through the import. A directory export carries no such requirement.

`--batch-size`: database records inserted per batch. Lower it when the import container is
OOM-killed part-way through a large archive.

enabled.description:
Run the import on the next start of the application pod.

**The target must be an empty installation.** The importer cannot merge into one that already
holds documents — it fails on the first document whose file is already on disk, part-way
through the copy — so this belongs on a fresh release rather than on one that has been serving
for a while. The import container checks for that up front and refuses to start, rather than
letting it happen half-way. To restore over an existing instance, delete the media and data
volumes first, so there is nothing left to collide with.

**An import that dies part-way is retried automatically.** The database load is an upsert and
re-runs cleanly, but the file copy refuses to overwrite what an earlier attempt already put in
place, so the next pod start clears that partial copy before importing again. What it deletes
is bounded by `restore.markerFile`: only a tree the chart itself verified empty and then wrote
into is ever cleared.

**The image version must match the one that produced the export.** An export carries an exact
image of the database, and the schema changes between releases; the importer warns about a
mismatch and then keeps going, which is the failure mode that costs an archive. Pin `image.tag`
to the source instance's version, import, then upgrade.
enabled.title: enabled

existingSecretKey.title: existingSecretKey

markerFile.description:
Name of the marker file written to the data volume once the import succeeds. Its presence
is what makes the import run exactly once; deleting it re-arms the import on the next restart,
which then fails against the now non-empty installation unless the volumes were cleared too.

A companion `<markerFile>.attempt` is written beside it *before* the import and removed on
success. Finding it on a later start is what tells the container an earlier attempt died
part-way, and is the only thing that lets it clear that attempt's partial copy and retry.
Deleting it by hand while a partial copy is on disk leaves the import unable to make progress.
